chapter.name: PythonTap Tutorial 3: An Object without Audio
chapter.header: PythonTap Tutorial 3: An Object without Audio
chapter.subhead: What a method returns is what the object outputs
chapter.body: Most Max objects are not audio objects: a bang asks for the next value, a list comes in and a list goes out, a number becomes a name. tap.python runs a Python class as such an object. It loads the class as tap.python~ does — attributes from its typed fields, messages from its methods, reloaded when saved — and adds one thing: what a method returns is what the object outputs.
Open the tutorial patcher, and turn on the audio to hear the rhythm.
The top of the patcher loads euclid.py:

A bang calls bang(), and the list it returns — a Euclidean rhythm, steps beats with pulses of them on, spread as evenly as they go — comes out of the left outlet. The metro bangs it on every step, so a change to steps or pulses is heard at once; zl.lookup picks the current step out of the list, and a 1 clicks.
The right outlet is the dumpout: getsteps outputs steps 8 from it, as any Max object with attributes does.
The middle of the patcher loads note_name.py:
chapter.code: def int(self, note: int) -> tuple[str, int]: return NAMES[note % 12], note // 12 - 1
chapter.body: The return hint, a tuple of two, gives the object two outlets, filled right to left as Max objects do: the octave, then the name. Play the keyboard. The name is a str, which the object outputs as symbol and the string — one symbol, whatever it holds — so sel matches it, and a message box's set $1 shows it.
The bottom loads scale.py, whose list method takes a whole list as one numpy array:
chapter.code: def list(self, values: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray: return values * self.factor + self.offset
chapter.body: A last parameter hinted np.ndarray — or list[float] — takes every argument of the message, and an array returned is output as a list.

A message runs on the thread it arrives on, as any object's does, and the method's result is output before the message returns, so trigger, metro and the rest work with it as usual. With Overdrive on, a metro's bangs arrive on the scheduler thread, which a long method holds while it runs; with Scheduler in Audio Interrupt also on, that is the audio thread, and the object says so in the console. Send such messages through deferlow to run them on the main thread.

tap.python outputs what a method returns: a number as a number, a str as a symbol, a list or an array as a list, and the values of a method hinted -> tuple[...] one per outlet. The help file and the PythonTap book have the whole table.
